title: Dense correspondence and interpretable skeletal morphospaces
introduction: Comparative skeletal biology seeks to relate anatomical variation to function and evolutionary history. The primate cuboid, a bone of the lateral midfoot, presents a demanding case: its joint surfaces, plantar tuberosity and peroneus longus tendon groove form a complex anatomy relevant to foot mechanics. Comparing this anatomy requires measuring differences across curved surfaces, articular margins and local relief, not only at isolated points.

sections.heading: The methodological gap
paragraphs: Three-dimensional scans capture detailed surfaces, but do not establish which locations correspond between specimens. Anatomical landmarks provide expert-defined anchors, yet may undersample variation between them. Dense matching addresses coverage, while learned shape spaces summarize variation; biological interpretation requires connecting both to inspectable anatomy. This study addresses that connection: how to build a quantitative morphospace from anatomically constrained dense matches and reconstruct the surface changes it represents.

sections.heading: A two-stage approach
paragraphs: Stage 1 uses landmark-adapted functional maps to estimate dense correspondences across a sparse network of specimens and templates. Anatomical anchors constrain the matches; surface diagnostics and targeted refinement address local discontinuities, collapse and incomplete coverage. This correspondence stage is part of the methodological contribution because errors in matching propagate into subsequent shape analysis.

Stage 2 synchronizes the maps into a common basis and trains an autoencoder, building on DISCO-AE and DiffusionNet, to encode and reconstruct complete skeletal surfaces. Principal-component analysis (PCA) summarizes variation in the learned codes. Decoding along those axes reveals the associated anatomical changes, linking statistical relationships among specimens to surface geometry.

sections.heading: Study scope and initial results
paragraphs: Anthropoid cuboids are the primary application. A non-fossil hominoid subset examines the same element within a narrower taxonomic range; mouse mandibles and humeri test the approach on different skeletal geometries. The current models produce reconstructed surfaces and decoded shape variation for all four datasets. These outputs make local contours, projections and depressions available for anatomical inspection alongside specimen relationships in the morphospace.

Earlier development analyses found agreement between learned shape relationships and manual-landmark and automated pseudolandmark morphometrics, with decoded cuboid axes localizing articular and plantar variation. These findings concern earlier model versions. Reconstruction, morphometric agreement, repeatability, phylogenetic signal and size associations are being reassessed for the revised datasets and models shown here.

sections.heading: Biological significance
paragraphs: The contribution is a connection between whole-surface measurement and anatomical explanation, complementing established geometric morphometrics. Instead of stopping at separation in a scatterplot, researchers can examine where and how surfaces differ and formulate explicit hypotheses about joint form, tendon pathways and skeletal diversity. Such hypotheses still require comparative or biomechanical tests: decoded variation alone does not establish locomotor adaptation or evolutionary causation.
